speechtext: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 55 to amend the Salary Deduction Act, 1932.

subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill provides that there shall be no deductions of the salaries, pay or compensation of any employee of the public service up to and including the sum of $1,000. That range takes in a very large number of employees of the public service. As nearly as we can ascertain some eighteen thousand in number will be affected, including revenue postmasters, part time collectors of customs, lighthouse keepers, wharfingers, charwomen, seasonal or part time labourers, lockmen and bridgemen on the canals. Those in receipt of salaries above the sum of $1,000 will be subject to the same deduction as hitherto.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT OF INQUIRY CONDUCTED BY HON. DONALD SUTHERLAND
speechtext:
In view of the observations that have
been made as to the public interest being safeguarded by the production of reports made under the Combines Investigation Act the motion will be accepted by the government, and I now produce and table the report in question. It is in part the report made under the Combines Investigation Act by the registrar to the Minister of Labour, dated March 4, 1933, and attached to that report of the registrar is the report of Mr. Sutherland. The report of Mr. Sutherland was not made pursuant to an appointment under order in council as was suggested the other day, because in looking into the matter I find he was appointed under another section of the act, but his compensation was fixed by an order in council, which order in council

Tobacco Industry
extended also to the compensation that was to be paid for similar services to various other persons named therein. I produce and table the document the more readily because in certain parts of this country it has been alleged that the report has been kept back because the Prime Minister of the country was largely interested as a shareholder of the Imperial Tobacco Company, and therefore was preventing this action being taken. I avail myself of this opportunity to say to this chamber that I am not either directly or indirectly through the intervention of a trustee or in any other way a shareholder of the Imperial Tobacco Company or any other tobacco company, and so far as I can ascertain never in all my life did I own a single share of that great undertaking.

speechtext:
I have a few observations
to make in connection with what happened last year when this same question was being discussed. I should like to quote what the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) said on March 21, 1933, with regard to the member for Temiscouata. These remarks appear on page 3500 of unrevised Hansard of that year. I have not yet received the bound copy of Hansard for last year and I must use the unrevised edition. The hon. minister said:
If the work carried on by the province of Quebec along these lines in the past needed defence, I defended them in the house against the impeachment of the hon. member for Temiscouata. Anyone who has even casual knowdedge of the history of the development of Canada should not be slow to commend the actions of the successive governments of the province of Quebec even before confederation, and in fact almost since the beginning of settlement, along this line.
Those were the observations which the minister made at the time. Immediately after he had uttered those words I rose to a question of privilege. I stated that I was sorry to interrupt the minister but I felt I had to object to his words. The minister continued on page 3501 as follows:
I am quite content to let the words of the hon. member for Temiscouata, as they will be revealed in the pages of Hansard, speak for themselves. If I used words which were not exactly his I can only say that of course my memory is not so good that I can follow him exactly. Certainly I gathered from his remarks to-day and a few days ago that he roundly condemned the administration of the colonization department of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Pouliot: By certain employees.
Mr. Gordon: The government takes responsibility for its officials, of course. The hon. member went so far as to say that the colonists who were sent out by the government had to eat grass and roots and so on, and I believe be even said they lived like swine. I do not come in contact with the provincial colonization men and I have nothing to do with provincial policies in Quebec, but I do know that this department is in touch with our committee, which consists of the representatives of the

Relief Act, 1934
colonization departments of the railways, of our department and of the Quebec department. From my observations and from what I can gather I cannot conceive that those men would be parties to a colonization effort such as has been described by the hon. member for Temiscouata.
When we were discussing the resolution upon which this bill is founded on March 22 I read a letter which had been sent to the Department of Labour by Reverend Father Beaulieu, the parish priest of St. Emile d'Auclair. That letter was published in English as an appendix to Hansard of March 26, 1934, page 1. I am not going to read the whole letter; I will quote just one paragraph. The Reverend Father Beaulieu says:
I have been patiently waiting, until this very day. It will take a miracle to save my settlers from starvation, that is the plain fact, with the few hundreds of dollars which I succeed in obtaining each month at the price of endless complaints and recriminations. The small children of settlers in my parish are without shoes, or stockings or clothes to cover themselves this winter to attend school (a large number cannot Rave the camps), they are in great distress, utter destitution-
The French word is "misere noire."
-a life of cruel disappointment for a poor missionary who is in charge of all these people.
This is an excerpt from the letter which I find in sessional paper No. 192, tabled on March 2 this year by the hon. gentleman. He has received that letter. Now, at the time he received it he had not yet given his approval to the relief works submitted to him by the provincial government of Quebec in August of last year, but he did so on the eve of this session, the very day before the opening of the session. Therefore, in giving his approval to the request made by the Quebec government on behalf of the settlers in the parish of Saint-Emile d'Auclair, he presumably regarded as well founded what was written by Father Beaulieu in his letter. That letter is a confirmation of what I said last year on behalf of the settlers, whose case is very serious. I would therefore ask the minister one question. Is he ready to admit that he was wrongly informed on March 21 of last year when he accused the member for Temiscouata of impeaching the province of Quebec by his statements in reference to the case of the settlers in that province and, in particular, in the county of Temiscouata?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Under the plan whereby the dominion government contributes, with the provincial government and with the municipality, $200 towards the settlement of a family, I find by reference to the schedule that only eleven families were settled in the
county of Temiscouata. I have a recollection of observations made by myself in the house last year in answer, I think, to a criticism made by the hon. member for Temiscouata with respect to the administration of the settlement of families. I tried to make it plain that the administration is entirely in the hands of the provinces-not only the province of Quebec but all the provinces. I also, if my recollection serves me correctly, took issue with the hon. member for Temiscouata as to the general success which I at least thought, and still believe, attended the plan. As regards criticisms that were offered at that time with respect to the administration, I can only repeat that it is the province of Quebec, or any other province that avails itself of the plan, which is charged with the responsibility of administration. I do not know that I can add anything to what I have just said.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I will readily admit that the minister is very clever; he evades the answer to my question, which was to the point. I did not discuss the question as to how many people had been put on the land in accordance with the plan in the county of Temiscouata. The question I asked was this: Does the hon. gentleman now admit that he was wrongly informed when on March 21 last year he declared to this house and this country that the member for Temiscouata had impeached his own province in his remarks on the colonization scheme in the province of Quebec and particularly in the county of Temiscouata? I ask the minister to answer that question in view of the fact that he has in his own files a letter from the Rev. Father Beaulieu, parish priest of Saint-Emile d'Auclair, repeating exactly what I said last year. May I ask the hon. gentleman to be good enough to answer my question, which is to the point.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I do not think it would add to the strength of the hon. gentleman's position if someone agreed with him in criticisms he may have made. We all have our own opinions; the hon. member has his and I have mine, and perhaps I am just as firmly grounded in my opinion as he is in his own. If that clause were to ibe dropped, it would shorten materially the further discussion of the measure. May I repeat what was said the other day? The clause did not appear, it was not found necessary, in the bill of the special session of 1930, though the session was called to deal with an alleged emergency. It appeared in the bill of 1931, but it was kept there only by the application of the closure on the part of the administration. In 1932, it was dropped, and nobody suffered as a consequence, no public interest suffered in the least. The next year it was reinserted, against the protests of hon. members on this side, but notwithstanding that it was there the minister has since told us that no use was made of it at all last year. He also told us that the only use made of the clause at any time was to allow banks and insurance companies to revalue

I submit that that does not justify the retention of the clause this year, particularly when, as I have already pointed out, it is known that in all probability this is going to be the year of a general election. And particularly, may I add, when the government is alleging that the emergency is pretty well gone by, that times are improved and conditions are now on the upgrade. There is therefore not the necessity for this alleged emergency legislation that there was before. If under these circumstances the minister does not withdraw the clause he must not wonder that we see an ulterior motive in its retention. As I pointed out, the clause is not to give the ministry power to legislate with respect to peace, order and good government; under the statutes they have already all the power needed for that purpose, but this clause is to give the ministry power, notwithstanding any law or any statute, to pass any measure it pleases by order in council, so long as the order in council may be designated one for the furtherance of peace, order and good government in Canada. As the minister has* shown us, the action with respect to the revaluing of securities was taken notwithstanding the existence on the statutes of provisions which gave the citizens of this country belief that securities having a certain value must be shown at that value when returns were being made with respect to them. I do not think the use to which the legislation has been put justifies its continuance. As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) said the other day, under the power being asked, the government during the period of a general election could pass any order in council it pleased with respect to something happening in the election, which might have a very vital bearing thereon. They might in effect repeal any section of the Dominion Elections Act. That cannot be denied, because the purpose of the clause is to give the governor in council power, notwithstanding the existence of any law or statute, to pass any order in council it pleases. I say for that reason alone we ought to oppose its retention to the limit. It is only too clear that with that power the government, under pressure, in the event of a dispute arising in some electoral district in the course of the campaign, could forthwith pass an order in council and settle the whole matter before the election day, could say that notwithstanding such and such a section in the election act, such and such is to be done. It cannot be denied that that power would be

given if this provision goes through. I cannot but believe that some purpose of that kind must be in the mind of the government, otherwise they would not retain the section at the present time. Not the election act only, but any legislation, no matter what it is, may be overridden. The government would be able to do for any corporation, for any organization, anything it pleased to designate as being done for peace, order and good government. No matter what the law of this country may be, it simply means that existing legislation, legislation enacted by parliament for the purpose of giving confidence in their rights and a sense of security to the public, is of no value at all; that there is no liberty, no right, that is not infringed by the power being given to the administration.
I have only heard the minister and hon. gentlemen on the other side give one other reason why the clause should be there, why that power should be given to the government at the present time, and to my mind it is a reason why it should not be there. It was that these are times of great social unrest. That is true. The world at the moment is passing through what may be and will be described in future as a social revolution and changes may come very rapidly. That being so, it is said that the government should be endowed with very special powers, to be able to act at any moment in regard to what may take place if something in the nature of revolutionary change came about.
One hon. member opposite, and I think the minister himself, referred to and gave as a reason for their adoption here the powers given to the president of the United States to deal with emergency conditions. May I first of all say a word with regard to the powers given to the president of the United States, in order to clear that up. The present president of the United States came into office about a year ago. He has had but one year of office; the powers given him were given only for a period of two years. But this administration is now completing its fourth year, it has had four years of power to inaugurate and carry into force the policies designated by it for the purpose of improving conditions. It has had a perfectly free hand in regard to those policies for all that time. It has had this extreme power given it on two previous occasions. As far as the United States is concerned, the president came into a situation which had been going, so it was alleged, from bad to worse, at least so we are led to believe, as a consequence of the inaction of the preceding administration. Here the situation was different. Here the government claims that

the situation has been improving right along, and that we are now into the fourth year of improvement as a consequence of their retention of office. So the parallel on that score does not hold. But the real point is this. As the minister knows and as hon. gentlemen opposite well know, the constitution of the United States is based on a wholly different principle from that underlying British parliamentary institutions. The executive of the United States is independent of the legislative body. The American system is a system of checks and balances, it is not a system of reconciling the wishes of the executive with those of parliament and vice versa. For that reason the parallel does not hold-
I am glad the Prime Minister has come in, because I would like, if I might, to speak directly to him on this point. We are discussing the second section of this relief bill; in it there is a clause by which the government asks to be given the power, notwithstanding any statute or law, to continue to pass orders in council with respect to peace, order and good government. I a,m trying to point out that the grounds for that legislation do not now exist. Whatever may have been said at previous sessions they do not exist now. According to the record, the government did not need nor ask for that power at the time of the special session of 1930, they got it in the session of 1931 only by use of the closure, it was dropped at the session of 1932 when according to the government's own statement conditions were much more serious than today, and no public interests suffered by it being dropped. In 1933 when it was restored it was against the strong opposition of this side of the house, and hon members in other parts of the house as well, but the power was never used last year, and we cannot see why the minister should ask for that power this year. The fact that this may be the year of a general election, which may occasion great uncertainty with respect to what is taking place in different parts of the country may increase the temptation for the government to use the legislation in ways that would not be followed if the pressure were less than is likely to be the case at the time of a general election.
The only real argument that has been urged in support of it is that these are times of great social unrest, that the world is passing through a time of social change. For my part I believe that it is so. I hope very much that far-reaching changes will come about and I believe they will. I hope they will result in a more equitable distribution of wealth, and mudi more in the way of social justice. I do

Relief Act, 1934
believe however that unless some country stands firmly for the preservation of its representative political institutions, institutions which have helped to preserve liberty and freedom, there is danger of every country being more or less submerged under the revolutionary tide which is sweeping across the world. Those who might otherwise greatly benefit by any social change brought about in an orderly and proper fashion would be the first to suffer by a change brought about in any other manner. We cannot stem the onward flow of the tide that has set in, but we can control and direct the channels through which it may be made to flow to the advantage and not to the ruin of all concerned.
The arguments urged by hon. gentlemen opposite are to the effect that the president of the United States has had to have exceptional powers; therefore similar powers should be given to our governor in council. When my right hon. friend entered the chamber I was saying that those powers were given to the president just a little more than a year ago. My right hon. friend and his ministers have now had nearly four years in which to shape matters and policies; as a consequence, I submit that so far as meeting any situation they are in a position very different from that of the president, when he assumed power. But apart from that-and this is the point I wish particularly to make-the executive in the United States does not bear the same relationship to the law making branch of government as does the executive in this country, or the executive functioning under British institutions anywhere. The executive in the United States is wholly independent of congress. Being independent where emergency powers are required it is necessary to give to the United States executive many powers which it is not at all necessary to give to an executive under our system of government where the executive is but a committee of the commons, and can obtain from parliament in virtue of its majority any legislation it may want or need.
The president of the United States cannot get the power he requires to deal with emergency conditions by going to the house of representatives and asking for it. He can only obtain what congress is prepared to grant. But my right hon. friend can. With the backing he now has he can come to this House of Commons and to meet a given situation may obtain whatever legislation is required. He may bring .parliament together at any time he desires, if it so happens that parliament is not in session. When it is in session he may anticipate a situation and get what he needs in order to meet it. That is a very different
state of affairs from the condition obtaining in the United States. I can well understand that in a country where the executive is wholly apart from congress, where no member of the ministry is on the floor of either house or in a position to explain a measure, it may be necessary in dealing with grave situations to have extreme powers given and to trust to their proper use. But that argument does not apply to the situation obtaining in Canada.
It has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite that there are dictators in Europe, and that the whole development on that continent is of a type which entrusts one or two men with complete authority to act quickly. I believe that is the very thing which is going to lead to much destruction throughout the world. I believe that to-day danger signals are being displayed in and sounded from almost every country in Europe, with the exception possibly of Great Britain. Great Britain is the exception because she has held more closely than any of the others to the parliamentary method of dealing with all situations.
I say that these movements for social change cannot be stopped. As a matter of fact we do not want to see them stopped, but we do want to see changes brought about in a way that will make human society a better human society not by methods which may lead to its total destruction. If change comes about without orderly development, or by means, and through channels which British parliamentary institutions through many centuries have helped to ensure as certain to be for the benefit of all, it may have a submerging effect, and men and institutions alike may be swept away before its uncontrolled advance. I could develop that thought at greater length, but I believe I have presented it sufficiently forceably to make my meaning clear to hon. gentlemen opposite. I do believe that this country of Canada, with a parliament fashioned on the model of free British parliamentary institutions, if it will but be true to itself and its heritage, may serve as an example to the nations of the world of how great social and industrial changes, in a period of world upheaval and unrest, can be brought about in the interests of the great body of the people, and without injury to any deserving interest. That is a great opportunity. I believe we can put through in orderly channels, and with the consent of the great body of the people all those measures required to effect far reaching change in the furtherance of human need, social justice and the common good.

Just one further thought in conclusion: it is that the consensus of view, the collective wisdom of the nation as a whole, is what parliament is able to bring to bear upon any great public question. That is a much greater safeguard to personal liberty and progress and to orderly change at a period of transition than 5s the view of any individual or group of individuals, who may be free to sit apart from parliament altogether, no matter how conscientious, earnest or sincere they maj^ be. It is for this above all other reasons that I appeal to the Prime Minister and his colleagues to withdraw this very subversive and dangerous section.

That, I repeat, is the purpose, no matter how you may try to conceal or glide over it by referring to peace, order and good government; the power which the government seeks is the power to legislate as it pleases, apart from parliament altogether and that notwithstanding any law or statute in existence in the country.

And what shall we have then? Instead of a number of representative assemblies laying down the laws of the country we shall have so many soviets established in different parts of Canada. I submit that all this is leading this country along entirely wrong lines; it is imitating the worst features of what has taken place in Europe and rejecting the best of what we possess. After all, what is the situation in Europe to-day? British system of representative government as we understand it and as it has developed through the years, and to have changes of the social order effected in a constitutional manner through that agency; not the destruction, as would otherwise be inevitable, alike of parliamentary institutions and the social order.
My criticism of this legislation is that it is baneful in the extreme because of the example it sets in matters of government. It is very serious, in my opinion, that this sort of legislation should again appear this year, and that an effort should once more be made to drive it through parliament. That was the reason-and I think the Prime Minister will credit me with sincerity in the position I took-I opposed this legislation so strongly at the outset. If he looks over what I said at the time, he will find that my main criticism was in the nature of the query: Where is this kind of thing taking us? Where are we going? That is the question the people of Canada will be asking themselves very soon in regard to this world revolutionary movement that is influencing this country as well as all others. So far, we have been more fortunate and in a better position than other countries, but with the rapid way in which thought is influencing action and conduct in different parts of the world, if men are going to imitate what is worst and throw out what is best in governmental methods, what hope is there for anyone ?
I have said all I intended to say on this section, but I say it with the deepest convic-ton and out of a fear that so far as Canada is concerned we are at this very time, to use once more a phrase that has been used in another connection, at the parting of the ways. We have to decide whether we shall stand for those institutions that have maintained liberty in the interests of all, and brought about and secured that liberty through their parliament as the palladium of liberty, or whether we are going to cease to have government conducted on a representative and responsible basis and go in for one or other of these extremes, the extreme of communism, on the one hand or of socialism or of fascism on the other.

Let me explain that long before the depression set in-perhaps a year or two-the government of New Brunswick passed an act in which, in order to encourage the opening up of more lands, they granted a bonus of eight dollars an acre to those farmers who would break up new lands, and who held titles to such lands. The reason the stipulation was made as to titles was to distinguish between the settler on crown lands who had not yet

obtained his title, and the established farmer. Under this provincial legislation the established farmer with one hundred acres of land, only forty or fifty acres of which was clear, and Who undertook to clear more of his land, received eight dollars an acre. When the depression set in and the federal government decided to aid unemployment by paying a percentage of the costs, the government of New Brunswick transferred this act so that it operated under federal aid. In 1931 fifty per cent of the $41,000 paid in connection with the clearing of this land was paid under the federal aid system and charged to unemployment relief. The federal Department of Labour certified and made the payments.
I suggest that this money could not have been paid as unemployment relief, because the farmers who received the eight dollars per acre were well to do; they did not require any relief in 1931. Prior to the depression years they received this money under legislation of New Brunswick which had for its purpose encouraging the opening up of more lands. Yet we find that fifty per cent of that is charged to and paid by the federal Department of Labour. I am pointing this out not so much to criticize the department but to show how necessary it is that care should be taken and every precaution exercised by the federal Department of Labour to see that the moneys voted by parliament are properly expended and not used for purposes for which they were not intended.

I agree with the hon. gentleman and think he is quite correct in stating that when the attention of the provincial government is drawn to any misapplication, if I may use that term, of federal funds, the refund will be made and likely has been made in the past. But that is all the more reason for the stand I take to-night, that there have not been sufficient safeguards surrounding the expenditure of federal aid money, not only in the province of New Brunswick but in other provinces, because it is rife throughout the dominion. I am not attacking only the province of New Brunswick. My hon. friend from York-Sunbury says that I am trying to besmirch the reputation of that province. I am not attempting to besmirch its reputation at all, but I do deprecate the idea of allowing such a misuse of public funds to go on as revealed here in the report of the auditor general. At any rate, I have the courage of my convictions and stand in this house to denounce that sort of thing, and that is more than the hon. member for York-Sunbury can say, because he is scared that in denouncing misdemeanours of that kind he will be reflecting on a government he so loudly praises and to which he is so solidly attached that he cannot see any good in those differing from him in political opinion. That is the only reason that prompts me to expose the matter. I drew the attention of the government to the state of affairs in 1932 and warned them then against certain misdemeanours am? '*ertain misappropriations of money, not by the individual who wanted to boodle or graft but by the provinces and municipalities who were using the money in a way in which it should not have been used, so that it did not reach the unemployed whom it should have reached.
Let me give you an instance of how unemployment relief is administered. Here again I wish to impress upon the minister that in making agreements with the different provinces he should be careful to stipulate what agreements these provinces shall make with the municipalities, and that the federal government shall have a word to say as regards the manner in which the municipalities are to distribute federal unemployment relief, instead of leaving it entirely to the provinces to deal with the municipalities. In the example I am going to give I am speaking of a
Relief Act, 1934

matter whereof I know. It became the practice in 1932 for them to go to a farmer and say, "You have lumber on your land. There are a lot of people who are too poor to buy wood and we want you to sell to us, the committee in charge of relief in this district, fifty or one hundred cords of wood. We will pay you fifty cents a cord as the wood stands. We will cut it and it will be hauled off your land." The farmer agrees to that and the wood is cut. The wood is not given to be hauled by the individual who really needs it for relief, but teams belonging to independent farmers are engaged to haul that wood at so much a cord. The cost of the wood when it reaches its destination amounts, including the fifty cents stumpage so-called, to $2.50 to $3 a cord to the municipal committee. The municipal committee, instead of distributing that wood to the poor and needy, sells it at so much a oord to some individual who undertakes to sell it to the public. He does not sell it to the unemployed because they have no money to pay for it, but when the municipal committee require wood they go to this individual and pay him $4 a cord for wood that they could have given to the needy person at a cost of $1.50 a cord. The federal government is asked to pay thirty-three and a third per cent of the cost of that class of relief work and the poor individual who is in need of wood does not get it until the municipality buys it back at the rate of $4 a cord from the individual to whom it had sold it at from $2.50 to $3 a cord. There is a great deal of wood needed among the poor people, especially if we have another winter like the one through which we are just passing. This shows that the minister should take particular care to give instructions to the provincial government that the agreements entered into oetween the provincial government and the municipalities shall, before becoming operative, be submitted to the Minister of Labour at Ottawa for his approval. If that system is adopted, the very misdemeanours, if I may so term them, to which I have just now referred, will be avoided.

Perhaps at this juncture
I might make some observations about the method that was pursued by the Department IMr. Veniot.]
of Labour in connection with the disbursement of unemployment relief funds. It may be recalled that in 1922 we had a similar sort of situation to that experienced in 1930, and the then government outlined a plan of assistance from the federal government to the provinces. This will be revealed in an order in council dated January 25, 1922, P.C. 191. I will ask the consent of the committee to have this order in council spread upon the record. It reads:

Certified copy of a report of the committee of the privy council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on the 25th January, 1922.
Privy Council Canada
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated 25th January, 1922, from the Prime Minister submitting the following observations with reference to the order in council of 7th October, 1921	(P.C. 3831),
respecting unemployment relief.
1.	The present administration, assuming office at the close of the year 1921, finds that a condition of unemployment beginning in the late months of 1920 and continuing throughout the year 1921 does not promise any material abatement during the early winter months of 1922.
2.	Consideration has been given to the means which would seem best adapted to the relief of the distress resulting from severe unemployment conditions, and the provisions to this end of P.C. 3831 have been carefully noted.
3.	The minister concurs in the view that the question of unemployment relief is fundamentally a municipal and provincial responsibility; that the abnormal economic and industrial conditions now existing and arising in a measure out of the late war alone afford justification for action on the part of the federal authorities; that federal action must therefore supplement municipal and provincial efforts, must be designed on lines permitting close and effective co-operation with and supervision by municipal and provincial authorities, and must be proportioned by the efforts of those authorities.
4.	That municipal undertakings in the nature of public works are important factors in meeting unemployment conditions, but such undertakings cannot be proceeded with during the winter months save at a considerably increased cost, which is in many cases beyond the financial resources of the municipalities.
5.	That, having these various points in mind, it is desirable that federal employment assistance and unemployment relief should be granted on the following basis:
(a)	In the case of public works undertaken by a municipality during the winter months and specially with a view to the relief of unemployment in the district, the municipality will bear the normal cost and the federal government will bear one-half of the extra cost incurred by the prosecution of the work during the winter season, the estimate of the normal cost to be approved by officers of the federal Department of Public Works; the federal grant to be conditional on the province assuming responsibility for one-third of such excess expenditure.

Relief Act, 1934
(b)	That where work cannot be provided, the federal government will refund to a municipality one-third of the disbursements made on account of unemployment relief, disbursed to others than those specified in paragraph (d) following and conditional on the participation on an equal basis by the province concerned.
(c)	That where in certain provinces there are unorganized districts without municipal government in which unemployment or distress exists and the provincial government finds it necessary to administer a system of unemployment or distress relief, the federal government will reimburse the provincial government concerned to the extent of one-half of such disbursements for relief and for the administration of the unemployment or distress relief policy in the district.
(d)	That in the case of unemployed former members of the Canadian or British forces, now in Canada, discharged as physically fit or not entitled to assistance by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, the federal government will reimburse the municipal authorities to the extent Of one-half the disbursements made for unemployment relief, the remaining quota to be contributed in equal parts by the province and municipality respectively.
6.	It is to be noted that these regulations do not seek to meet the case of disabled members of the Canadian overseas forces and other classes of returned soldiers which fall within the jurisdiction of regulations administered by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; or of persons (where such exist) whose necessities do not clearly arise from inability to secure employment and with whose necessities the municipal authorities have been accustomed to deal.
7.	It is the expectation of the federal authorities that the provisions herein will be interpreted broadly and generously by the municipalities and the provinces so that no resident of Canada willing and able to work and unable to secure employment shall lack food, clothing or shelter for himself or herself and dependants.
8.	These provisions to continue in effect until the close of the present fiscal year.
The committee concur in the foregoing observations and recommendations and submit the same for approval accordingly.
(Sgd.) Rodolphe Boudreau,
Clerk of the Privy Council.

In the fall of 1930 after many conferences between the Department of Labour and the auditor general with respect to the best method to be employed in order to safeguard the federal treasury and after this certificate was agreed to, the auditor general wrote to the deputy minister of labour in a letter dated November 5, 1930, as follows:
Dear Sir:
In reply to your letter of the 29th ult. enclosing a form of certificate w'hich it is proposed to send to the various provinces to be filled in as indicated thereon with the particulars of all projects undertaken by the various provinces and municipalities claiming aid from the federal government under the Unemployment Relief Act, 1930, 21 George Y, chap. 1, I am of opinion that if the particulars asked for thereon are carefully prepared and signed by the appropriate provincial officers, the information thus provided will be sufficient for my purposes.
"The appropriate provincial authorities," it seems to me, are such as may be designated by the provincial government. I would consider it more satisfactory if the provincial auditor were one of the signatories to the certificate.
And in order that the Labour department might follow the direction of the auditor as disclosed in the letter I have just read, the certificate was required to be signed by the respective provincial auditors. Undier the terms of this arrangement which was agreed to, certified to, and approved by the auditor general, the administration of the act of 1930 was carried on. I hold no brief for the auditor general, neither do I want unduly to criticize his activities, but under his direction this work has been projected; all these accounts are certified to first in the department, then by the auditor general's department, and the cheques were countersigned by the auditor general. During the year 1931 some irregularities were disclosed; I do not suggest for a moment that they amounted in any way to a deliberate attempt to defraud either the federal treasury or any other. The administration of unemployment relief has been a most difficult and complex matter, giving rise to many baffling situations not only to the federal government but to the municipalities and the provinces, and in my business experience I have never seen any work so well and unselfishly administered. There have been but few instances of people who so forgot their duty and disregarded their responsibilities as to transgress. Generally

Relief Act, 1934
and broadly speaking the administration of the moneys of the taxpayers, municipal, provincial and federal, has been free from any sort of pilfering or looting such as suggested by some hon. members.
However, a time came when certain irregularities appeared, and the attention of the auditor general was drawn to them. It came to a head with respect to Port Alfred in Chicoutimi county. The director of unemployment relief notified the auditor general that he thought it desirable that a further investigation, outside of the then prevailing practice, should take place with respect to that municipality and some others that seemed to be in a similar condition. Now what happened'? Apart perhaps from a test audit, nothing was done until September; 1932, when order in council P.C. 2163 was passed by the executive. With the leave of the committee I would like to put this upon the record. In giving directions to the auditor general the order in council states: In view of the foregoing,-
That is, after reciting the necessity for further audit.

Then further on:
The minister further recommends that the auditor general be authorized to investigate the provincial systems of auditing municipal relief accounts, to the end that the dominion government may be satisfied that the municipal accounts put forward by the provinces are in accordance with the agreements entered into between the dominion government and the provin ces.

14.	That the unemployment relief branch has relied upon the auditor general for any necessary additional audit as the staff of the branch does not include personnel necessary to carry out an audit in the field.
In view of the foregoing, the minister recommends that the auditor general be authorized to conduct such audit of provincial accounts, in connection with unemployment relief expenditures, as he deems essential to safeguard the interests of the dominion treasury;
And that the commissioner of unemployment relief and the auditor general be authorized to accept from the provinces accounts rendered under clause 6 of the agreements under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, 1931, and to provide for dominion contributions to such accounts irrespictive of whether such accounts cover what are known as local improvement works to which the local proprietors will eventually contribute, or otherwise;
And that, further, the commissioner of unemployment relief and the auditor general be authorized to accept accounts from the provinces under clause 1 of the agreements entered into under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, 1931, and to pass for payment the accounts for the dominion contribution to the expenditures reported by the provinces as having been made by the municipality, including in such municipal expenditures amounts voluntarily contributed by individuals, business firms, or associations, to the municipality, providing that such amounts have been utilized solely for relief purposes, and have been expended under the jurisdiction of the municipal authorities; and provided that such funds have not been raised by arbitrary deductions from wages payable to those engaged on relief work.
The minister further recomends that the auditor general be authorized to investigate the provincial systems of auditing municipal relief accounts, to the end that the dominion government may be satisfied that the municipal accounts put forward by the provinces are in accordance with the agreements entered into between the dominion government and the provinces.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendations and submit the same for approval.
(Sgd.) E. J. Lemaire,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
Then, on May 31, 1933, the dominion director of unemployment relief received this letter from the auditor general:
Re: Port Alfred, Chicoutimi County I have your letter of May 22, in which you request that I audit the accounts of relief expenditures rendered by the province in respect to the town of Port Alfred, and informing me that you are placing the municipality on the "stop-payment" list until such time as I report on the audit.
When I requested my chief investigator to inform you that my representatives were about to continue their investigations in Quebec. I had in mind that if there was some particular municipality that you thought should be investigated, I would include it among those which, in due course, I intended to examine.

Port Alfred might be one of these municipalities. Under present conditions, however, would it not be advisable to have the provincial auditor make a special local audit of the accounts of that municipality and report thereon before further federal payment may be made?
Bear in mind that this letter is dated May-31, 1933; the first order in council was in September, 1932, and this is the answer that comes from the auditor general to the Labour department. The letter continues:
That audits of certain municipalities should be made at your specific request, and that the making of payments should be contingent upon my report, would not only interfere with the independent functioning of the audit office, but might possibly work a hardship on the municipality concerned.
You will understand that, in the circumstances, I cannot assume the obligation of making an immediate audit of the municipality named.
Yours very truly,
Geo. Gonthier,
Auditor General.
That letter was directed to the dominion commissioner of unemployment relief and was referred to me; and in answer to it I wrote to the auditor general on June 7, 1933, in the following terms:
Re: Port Alfred, Chicoutimi County, P.Q.
The dominion commissioner of unemployment relief has brought to my attention his communication to you regarding the above, dated May 22, also your reply of May 31.
I observe that it is your view that the making of audits of certain municipalities at the request of this department would interfere with the independent functioning of the audit office and in your opinion "might possibly work a hardship on the municipality concerned."
I understand from the commissioner's letter of May 22, that your representative informed him that you were proceeding with an audit of accounts in certain municipalities and that you would like to have the names of municipalities suggested to you by the commissioner, whose views on this point would naturally be helpful, and I understand that it was in accordance with this request and in the spirit of cooperation that the commissioner suggested that an audit be carried out of the municipal accounts at Port Alfred.
I cannot agree that the submission of the name of this or any other municipality to you in reply to your request would interfere with the "independent functioning of the audit office," nor can I conceive why it could "possibly work a hardship on the municipality concerned." Indeed I would assume that your first concern would be for the interests of the federal government rather than for the municipality.
I observe your statement that in the circumstances you cannot assume the obligation of making an immediate audit of the municipality named. I do not know what circumstances you refer to other than that you refuse to make the audit because the commissioner has suggested it. As I have above stated, the suggestion was
Relief Act, 1934
made at the request of your representative, and an audit which may be necessary should not be omitted because in your opinion it might possibly work a hardship on the municipality concerned, or for any other reason that I am aware of.
Yours truly,
W. A. Gordon,
Minister of Labour.
Then there is a reply dated June 23, 1933, from the auditor general. It is addressed to myself, and is as follows:
I am in receipt of your letter of June 6 regarding the audit of relief expenditure and of another of the 7th received in this office on the 19th, with special reference to the municipality of Port Alfred, P.Q.
I am naturally anxious to avoid any misunderstanding which might arise out of informal conversations and correspondence concerning the audit of a class of expenditure having its own special problems of administration and' control. In the circumstances, and in order to avoid any doubt as to my intentions concerning cooperation, I am making a broad review of the whole question after which I shall write to you at greater length.
I sincerely hope that it may be possible to arrive at an acceptable solution of our problems consistent with the designedly limited duties and responsibilities of the auditor general as defined by statute and with the administrative limitations under which this office has been labouring for some time past.
Assuring you of my desire to assist in any way possible in coping with the great difficulties arising out of the administration of unemployment relief.
I am,
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) Geo. Gonthier,
Auditor General.
On June 28, 1933, I replied to that letter in these terms:
I am in receipt of your letter of June 23 and note your anxiety to avoid any misunderstanding which might arise out of informal conversations and correspondence concerning the audit of relief expenditures. I must confess I do not altogether grasp what misunderstanding you have in mind which might occur in this regard. To my mind there would appear to be no ambiguity or ground for doubt as to the duties and obligations which devolve upon yourself and staff in this matter.
The terms of P.C. 2163 of September 30, 1932, are clear and devoid of any ambiguity. It contains specific instructions provided for in section 62 (g) of The Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. being chapter 178 of the R.S.C. 1927, from which I quote as follows:
"The auditor general shall examine and audit, if required so to do by the Minister of Finance, and in accordance with any regulations which are prescribed for his guidance in that behalf by the treasury board, . . .
(g) any other public accounts which, . . . the treasury board directs him to examine and audit."
The disbursements under the consecutive relief acts having reached such proportions
Relief Act, 1934

made it necessary, in the judgment of myself and colleagues, to pass the said order in council in which we have set out specific instructions to yourself as auditor general. From that order in council I quote two clauses, of which I am confident you have already taken full cognizance:
" The minister recommends that the auditor general be authorized to conduct such audit of provincial accounts, in connection with unemployment relief expenditures, as he deems essential to safeguard the interests of the dominion treasury."
"The minister further recommends that the auditor general be authorized to investigate the provincial systems of auditing municipal relief accounts to the end that the dominion government may be satisfied that the municipal accounts put forward by the provinces are in accordance with the agreements entered into between the government and the provinces."
There can be no doubt as to the government's intent contained in these instructions, and I am at a complete loss to understand why there can exist in your mind any lack of comprehension as to their import. They call for you to conduct such audit of provincial accounts as you deem essential to safeguard the interests of the dominion treasury. These instructions were given you in September, 1932, and now, nine months later, you advise the dominion commissioner that, owing to certain embarrassments which you fear it might cause some of the municipalities, you are loath to take the necessary steps by way of audit which would carry out those instructions.
With great diffidence and great reluctance I am compelled to state that your department has not complied with the expressed intention of the government in a matter of very vital and national importance. Ministers of the crown, particularly at a time like this, must of necessity rely upon the various departments of government which are charged with the responsibility of seeing that the policies of the government are carried out, and there is no department which should be more astute to recognize the necessity of activity, and be more zealous in its activity, than that of the auditor general, when the federal government is making contributions in vast sums out of the federal treasury to the provinces of Canada, who with their creatures, the municipalities, alone are the agents to expend the money so contributed.
X write this letter, as I have above stated, with the greatest reluctance but, in the light of our previous interviews and correspondence and the attitude you have taken, I am regretfully forced to the conclusion that you either are not seized of the national importance of conducting your audit in accordance with the instructions of the government as contained in P.C. 2163, or that you entertain views with respect to the same which are in conflict with the spirit and terms of the order in council, and have decided to adopt a course of your own fashioning.
Yours very truly,
W. A. Gordon.

What was the reply from the auditor general?
Mr. 'GORDON: I do not believe there was a reply. This is the order in council to which

the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) made reference on March 26 last. On that occasion he made statements, probably not with a desire to misrepresent in any way but purely through inadvertence. From his observations it would seem that action by the Dominion government was taken only on March 12, 1934. As a matter of fact action had been taken in the fall of 1930, and in each succeeding month the closest sort of check was made, as I have indicated.
The fall of 1930?
Does the minister mean 1932?
What is the date of the letter the minister has just read?
The letters I have read will appear in Hansard.
I should like to have the date, so that we may follow what is now being said.

The last letter I read was dated June 28, 1933. When the right hon. gentleman opposite was speaking on March 26 last no doubt he believed that the first action taken by the government was taken on March 12, 1934. However, if one reads the order in council a little more carefully he will not labour under that misapprehension. It is as follows:
Whereas the Relief Act, 1932, empowers the governor general in council, notwithstanding the provisions of any statute of law, inter alia, to enter into agreements with any of the provinces respecting relief measures therein, and also (in addition to such relief and other measures specified in the said act), to take all such other measures as might be deemed necessary or advisable for carrying out the provisions of the said act;
And whereas agreements having been entered into with the various provinces of Canada respecting relief measures therein under the authority of the Relief Act, 1932, and other measures of relief undertaken under the antecedent legislation respecting unemployment relief and need having arisen in consequence for the conduct of audits of provincial accounts relating to relief expenditures and the investigation of the provincial system of auditing municipal relief accounts, it was directed by order in council, dated September 30, 1932 (R.C. 2163), passed under the authority of the Relief Act, 1932, that:
Then it goes on to embody in the order in council of March 12, 1934, what was recited in the order in council passed over two years before. So if the right hon. leader of the opposition in making his observations a few

Relief Act, 1034
nights ago had gone through the order in council passed on March 12 he would have seen there a clear and distinct reference to the earlier order in council to which I have made reference, and would not have fallen into the error which he did.
I do not want to detain the members of the committee but I want to say in fairness to the municipalities, in fairness to the provinces, in fairness to the Labour department and in fairness to the taxpayers of this country, that the federal Labour department has taken every reasonable step to see that the moneys provided by the taxpayers were applied for the purposes for which parliament enabled this government to make the moneys available. If the suggestion that the treasury has been looted goes out to the taxpayers it only adds to their anxieties, and I could not therefore refrain from shortly spreading on the record just what the situation is. I can only repeat that if there was looting then every little village council, every town and city council, every provincial government and the federal government are all looters together. I do not think anyone would care to subscribe to any such idea as that. I think, Mr. Chairman, that the members of this committee should have this record spread on Hansard in order that anxieties that may have arisen in the minds of the taxpayers of this country should be allayed to the extent at least that these official records disclose that the government has endeavoured to have audits made from the very beginning right down to date of such a kind and character as were approved of, as they were, by the auditor general.

After listening to what the minister has said I feel pretty sure that one is not wide of the mark in saying that it is a case of endeavouring to lock the door after the horse has been stolen. It is all very well for the minister to come along to-day and say, "We asked the auditor general to do this and that," when at the time these original agreements were being entered into the Prime Minister himself said on three or more occasions in this house, in answering the opposition when we were advocating the auditing of the accounts, that it would be an insult to ask the governments of the provinces to permit the accounts to be audited. I think the minister heard my statement the other day but perhaps the Prime Minister was not in when I read what the Prime Minister said at that time. His words were quite distinct. For example, at page 173 of Hansard of 1930 the Prime Minister is reported as having said:
Are we to be told, because two or three members of this house stand up and complain
of a provincial legislature that therefore we are to insult that legislature by saying that we are to deal with their affairs and not our own? Are we to mind our business or their business?
And at page 175 the Prime Minister is reported as having said:
I will look further into the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition-
That was that great care should be taken to see that the accounts were audited.
-.but I cannot conceive how, under our constitution. any self respecting province would expect the dominion government to place upon it what I regard as an unenviable and unnecessary insult by saying:
This was the proposal in the form of a section that I had suggested should be included in any agreement made with the provinces:
Where any moneys are expended under this act by way of contribution to provinces, municipalities or other bodies, the auditor general shall audit the expenditure made by the province, municipality or other body, and shall report thereon to parliament within thirty days after the commencement of the next session.
That was the clause which we suggested should go into the bill relating to the expenditure of public moneys for purposes of relief, and the Prime Minister himself said that it would be an insult to the provinces to insert any such clause. Again at page 164 the Prime Minister said:
This parliament has no jurisdiction to interfere with the provinces and the municipalities in the expenditure of their moneys. If that were made a condition I think it would be regarded by the provinces as an insult.
As I pointed out at the time it was federal moneys that were referred to, not the moneys of the municipalities or the provinces, but money going out of the federal treasury, and the government could attach to the expenditure of that money any condition it pleased. It would not have interfered with the powers of the provinces or of the municipalities in the slightest degree. They did not have to take our money. It was, however, our duty to the public who had to pay the shot to see that with respect to any money to be spent there were adequate audits. I venture this prediction, that in the agreements which the minister entered into with the provinces it is not specifically set out that every dollar of public money from the federal treasury to be spent for purposes of relief shall be audited by a federal auditor. The minister reads correspondence between himself and the auditor general which took place after several millions of public moneys had been expended-

A great deal of money had been spent, as the minister well knows, within the very first year.

That is the
point. It was public money and it was the business of my right hon. friend and his colleagues in spending federal money to see that every bit of expenditure was audited down to the last payment. But as I say the minister reads correspondence with the auditor general asking him to do certain things which, with the staff he had, I presume it would have been to some extent physically impossible for the auditor general to do. What should have been done, as we suggested from the very first, was that the expenditure of these millions of dollars, now over one hundred million, should have been entrusted to a national commission which would have exercised careful supervision and none had auditors who would have reported to parliament. Then we should have had proper auditing.
To begin with, to expect the minister's department to deal with this whole question of unemployment relief was a mistake. The department was established to carry on business in a normal way in normal times, and there has never been, despite its increases, the staff necessary to begin to handle unemployment relief. The first Minister of Labour, as hon. members recall, worked as conscientiously as any minister could have done to carry out his duties, and with what result? He broke down completely and is now no longer here. It was impossible from the first that any minister could take on the task he did with the staff he had and attempt to do it satisfactorily, with due regard for the public interest. The mistake made was that the government did not at the outset grasp the significance of the unemployment problem.

If they did, they never took the steps necessary to see that relief was properly administered. When next the Prime Minister made the statement that it would be an insult to the provinces to expect to have any auditing done, it was in the public mind inviting the expectation of the freest kind of distribution of public funds. It was not until after this that the minister corresponded with the auditor general and sought to put an impossible task upon him. The fact that the auditor general even by a cursory visit of his officials to different communities had no difficulty in unearthing the evidence which he did of waste on a colossal scale is conclusive proof of the inadequacy of the measures taken by the government, and the fact that such waste was possible at all can only reflect on the administration because they alone are responsible for it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am very grateful for
this opportunity to deal with this situation. The right hon. gentleman would have us believe that his .anxiety for the public interest is so great that he must cry aloud to high heaven that money has been wasted and that the taxpayer has been defrauded. He practically charges theft against the provincial and municipal authorities. Let us see what are the facts. In 1930 when he suggested in this chamber that adequate provision was not being made to safeguard the public interest with respect to expenditures to which the dominion was contributing, we declined absolutely to deal with municipalities. There was no point of contact between the municipalities and this government except through the provincial governments. At that time we did not undertake by agreement or otherwise to do other than make a contribution to expenditures by the provincial authorities. When it was suggested that we should audit the accounts of the provinces I said that they -being autonomous units, that would be little short of an insult. I had high authority for saying that. In 1922 the right hon. gentleman had to deal with the problem and he passed an order in council in which he pointed out the difficulties of the situation. I hold in my hand the form of certificate which was settled upon by his government, not with t'he provinces but with the municipalities to whom contributions were made. That certificate was to be signed by the municipal treasurer and, what minister does the committee think? It was not a commission, it was not a denial of responsible government; oh, no, we are going to have responsible government when we are in power, and have it through our ministers. But when

we are in opposition we want a commission and thereby destroy the theory of responsible government. That is the view of the right hon. gentleman. The Minister of Labour, the Honourable Mr. Murdock, was to certify and the treasurer of the municipality was to sign. There is the form under which the provincial auditor then gave his certificate and our auditor paid.
I was so impressed with what was said in 1930 that before I left for England I gave certain instructions as to how I thought the matter should be looked after. The late Senator Robertson sought, through his deputy to safeguard the federal treasury in his dealings with the auditor general and the preparation of the provisions of the agreements which were made. In the correspondence we find a letter written by the auditor general to Mr. Ward. I ask the committee to note the date of this letter. It was dated November 5, 1930, before any considerable money had been spent. The letter reads in part:

We will point that out in a minute. In 1931 there was an expansion of activity and the agreements between the provinces and the dominion contemplated larger expenditures by the municipalities. The min-

ister, not being able to get the certificates he was looking for for his own safety and the safety of the government, took it up with the auditor general, the person with whom he should take it up. I ask any hon. member to read that correspondence and tell the committee what he thinks of it. The auditor general was fearful that it might involve difficulty with the municipalities but he was reminded by the minister that his duty was to the dominion taxpayer and not to the municipality. That is what we complained of. Everything that could be done was done for the purpose of having the federal official appointed by law do his duty and protect the taxpayer in accordance with the terms of a certificate with which he said he was satisfied. He replied that he was fearful that it might involve difficulties with the municipalities.
He is a servant of this house.

Why was it not brought to the attention of the house before?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It has been; the papers have been laid on the table. If the hon. gentleman will read them he will see exactly what they indicate. I have no quarrel with the auditor general but I have a quarrel with an official who, when asked for his views, outlines the method by which the work should be done and when it is done in accordance therewith and he is asked, re-asked and asked again to put this matter in such shape as will not leave any doubt, then files what he calls an audit and says that the officials of the municipalities and provinces are really thieves. That is his suggestion. I say that you have no right to say that the mayor of Fredericton, New Brunswick is a wrongdoer because he devoted a portion of the money which he expended to medical relief and then asked the dominion to pay a share. As soon as it was pointed out that that was wrong, he undid it. It is as wrong as it possibly could be to make that assertion.
The check which is being carried on in connection with these accounts by the minister and his department has been for the purpose of inducing the auditor general to do his duty. It is a nice mess that we have to face when the auditor general, over whom the government has no control, through these test audits and letters which he wrote, has made it appear that the government has failed in its duty when, in fact, the government has continued to ask him to do his duty and he has failed to do it.

Did the right hon. gentleman not state in the house that

it was not the duty of the government to have an audit of the provincial and municipal accounts?	.

speechtext: That was not the kind of agreement.

If the
formula that my hon. friend has read was followed, I cannot see anything particularly wrong with it. If the auditor should proceed against the will of the government, as expressed by the Prime Minister in the House of Commons, it would be a curious state o affairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is his duty when he thinks he is right.
My right hon. friend is straining the point to a very considerable degree to-night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not. I say, it is his duty.
That is my impression and I am entitled to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is wholly wrong for the Prime Minister or any other minister to interfere with the auditor general, and I have made it my duty not to interfere with or to suggest to him what he should do, and the correspondence, if it is desired, will prove that conclusively. The Minister of Labour, in the submission he made to him with the approval of the government, indicates clearly the position which he took, namely, that you cannot blow hot and cold, that you cannot tell us what course to pursue one day and, when we pursue it, say it is wrong. If there is anything wrong in connection with this the wrong rests with the auditor general of Canada and not with us. What is more, when in 1930 I made the statement I did, it was a correct statement and one which I would repeat; but in consequence of the character of the agreements that were made, and the extension of our activities in the finding of money for direct relief and for work in the municipalities, we believed that it was desirable that the auditor general should exercise closer supervision. In consequence-I will say frankly-of what the right hon. gentleman said in 1930, I wondered if my view of this situation could by any possible chance be in error and if you will refer to what he did in 1922 under similar circumstances and compare his agreement with this, you will see in our certificate safeguards for the dominion which were not dreamed of in the certificate of 1922. His account was with the municipalities; ours was not, for we dealt

with the provinces. We insisted upon their auditor giving a certificate that the money indicated had been spent and that the municipality had made its contribution, whereupon our obligation arose, under the agreement, to make our contribution in accordance with the terms of that agreement, which we did.
I have no reason to believe that the auditors of the various provinces are not honest men; I have no reason to believe that the certificates which they certify to as being correct are bogus certificates. But I am asked . to believe that these certificates, signed as they are by the auditors of the respective provinces, are fraudulent. That is what I am asked to believe to-night, and I decline to believe it. That errors may have arisen would be expected in an expenditure so vast, and wherever they have been detected and any injury has been suffered by the exchequer of Canada the wrong has been undone and the remedy made by the action of the provinces themselves. Now, those are the facts. Talk about locking the door after the horse is stolen! Why, it was the very fear I had, in consequence of the way in which the right hon. gentleman had spoken, that before I left these shores in October I asked that the Minister of Labour should give this matter more than ordinary attention, and the form of certificate as compared with the certificate issued in 1922, indicates the extent and character of the real care that was taken to prevent any difficulties arising on that score. And I say now, test audits or no test audits, that I do not believe that in the city of Fredericton, the mayor of which is a gentleman of the high character of Mr. Clark, or in any municipality in this country there has been a deliberate effort on the part of anyone to gouge the dominion taxpayer. I do not believe that the auditor of the province of Quebec or of Ontario or of Prince Edward Island or of New Brunswick or of Nova Scotia or the western provinces would sign a certificate for the purpose of fraudulently taking money from the dominion taxpayers, and that is what I am asked to believe; for there is the certificate, the form of which is such that if the auditor general felt that i was insufficient his duty was to point out to us wherein it might be changed. The hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray) asks, why did I feel that there was any possible difficulty about this and that the auditor general should give it further attention. I will tell him why.

A guilty conscience.
