That is the point exactly, and that is what the certificate points out, that the money must have been expended before our share was paid. So that before there could be any fraud practised against the dominion there must also be fraud practised against the province and the municipality. And if we t-ook the certificate of the provincial auditor, and he in turn took the authority of the proper officer of the municipality, we had three safeguards: (1) This certificate, which is No. 1 so far as we are concerned; (2) The signature of the provincial auditor; and (3) The certificate given by the proper officer of the province pledging the fame and good name and reputation and honour of the province to the validity and justice of the claim.
Now I submit to the committee that inasmuch as it would be asking the dominion auditor to audit the accounts of all municipalities and provinces it would be putting
Relief Act, 1984

upon him-and I repeat what I said in 1930- a burden which is not contemplated by the constitution; for all that he would have to be sure of would be the expenditure of our money. Now our money was not spent like other money. Our money was to be paid to the province to reimburse the province for expenditures actually made by them, or the municipalities, the creatures of the provinces; and when a certificate in that form was produced, certified to by an auditor, with the good name and fair reputation of the province behind it, the province itself signing, then I submit that this is the greatest possible safeguard you could have. And if test audits showed that the precautions taken by the auditor general to secure the Dominion of Canada's taxpayers from exploitation were inadequate, why did he not respond with some sort of suggestion in answer to all the inquiries made of'him? That is my objection. There is the record, and he who runs may read.
We have no apology nor excuse to offer- neither one nor the other. In 1930, as soon as the act came into force, we took up with the dominion auditor, appointed by statute, not amenable to any government, the method that should be pursued for the purpose of safeguarding the public treasury against exploitation. The contributions made by the dominion were made not for the purpose of getting vouchers for work done here and there, but as contributions to work undertaken by the provinces and municipalities in discharging their constitutional duties. In every instance the papers that came in were checked and rechecked by the Department of Labour just as in 1922 for services of a similar character the checking was done by the late administration. When the documents were so checked, supported by the vouchers and by the certificates of the auditor of the province and an officer speaking for the good name, honour and reputation of the province, we felt safe. What is more, if it subsequently develops that there have been overpayments, we know quite well that there will be no difficulty in having such overpayments refunded because the security that comes to us by reason of the name of the province being attached to the document as well as the check of the auditor general renders it impossible for this country to be defrauded of a single cent, and every cent that investigation or audit indicates has been paid in excess of what is right, just and proper under the terms of the agreement, will be reimbursed to the treasury of Canada. About that there need be no possible doubt. In the meantime we

anxiously await some suggestion from the auditor general, for whom it is very easy to produce the result of a test audit here or there; but with respect to the tens of millions of dollars that have been expended it will be found on analysis and investigation that the cases in which wrongdoing has been done wilfully or purposely by auditors of provinces, meaning that they must be parties to a conspiracy to defraud the taxpayers of Canada, or by municipalities, meaning that mayors of towns and cities have aided and abetted conspiracies for the purpose of defrauding the public, are very few, for I have no more right to assume that an auditor of a province or the mayor or chief magistrate of a municipality is derelict in his duty or fraudulently inclined or given to conspiracy than I would have that any dominion official under similar circumstances is not similarly inclined.

The Prime
Minister has apparently at last wakened up to the fact that the treasury has been looted and is doing his utmost to load the blame on to the shoulders of the auditor general, an officer of parliament who is not here to speak for himself.

I need not go further than my right hon. friend's own words this evening to show where the full responsibility rests. He has admitted that there has been need for more in the way of auditing and that money has been wasted.

speechtext: I deny that statement positively.
My right hon. friend does not admit it even yet.

Perhaps he will give the house a special committee to investigate the expenditures of these moneys, and particularly the charge that the auditor general is responsible for what has occurred. We shall then have the whole matter investigated and find out where and how the public moneys have gone. If this is done, I venture to say that it will be one of the most shocking stories with which the country has ever been faced.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There will be no "valley of humiliation" so far as we are concerned.

If the Prime Minister will kindly retain his seat while I am speaking, I shall be much obliged. I just

wish to repeat that we need not go further than what the Prime Minister has said to-night to make quite clear where the whole responsibility rests for any overexpenditure or waste or stealing of public money there has been in connection with this $100,000,000 that has been voted for purposes of relief. In this regard it is important to bear in mind that the statement which the minister laid on the table the other day indicates that the sum of $110,000,000 has been spent out of the public treasury for the purposes of relief, distributed in the different ways the minister has described.
That was in four years.

Yes, in four years by this government since it came into office. In addition to that there have been loans to the provinces amounting to $52,000,000 and guarantees of one kind or another to the extent of $111,000,000, making altogether something like $274,000,000 which this government has either spent or loaned or guaranteed in connection with unemployment relief. What does the Prime Minister say to-night? I took his words down at the time; he said: "We did not agree to deal with the municipalities." Whose fault was that? Was that the fault of the auditor general, or was it the responsibility of the Prime Minister and his government? Why did they not agree to deal with the municipalities?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Because it is improper.
Now my right hon. friend says: We did not do it because a previous government did not do it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that. The right hon. gentleman is wrong. Because the memorandum produced a moment ago was a receipt by a municipality I said that we did not deal with municipalities because it was improper to do so.

I disagree
entirely with the Prime Minister when he says that it would have been improper to do so. The government could deal with anybody it pleased, in any way it pleased. It was its duty In such a situation to see that the right method was taken to protect the public treasury. The Prime Minister said: We discovered there were certain certificates which were given by the provinces, which were accepted by a previous administration as evidence that the money given to the municipality was properly spent. He exhibited a photostat copy of a provincial certificate and said: Ours was like that, seeking to have it appear that in following the previous administration they were doing all that could properly be expected of them.
What were the facts in regard to the action taken by the previous administration? After the great war, when soldiers were being reestablished in civil life, large numbers of men were unemployed and the municipalities and provinces found it impossible to obtain occupations for many who were coming back from overseas. The then federal government, not the late Liberal government, but the previous Conservative or Unionist administration, followed by the Conservative administration of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, undertook to aid the provinces in assisting the municipalities in finding work for the unemployed, and adopted a system of voting sums of money as grants in aid to those provinces to further public works to enable unemployed to be put to work. When the change of government took place in December, 1921, we were faced with having to carry on this relief which had been introduced by the previous administration and we were unable to adopt a different system while the period of the fiscal year remained what it was. But as leader of the government of the day, I at once intimated to the provinces that we intended to discontinue this practice as soon as possible and that we felt the time had come when the provinces, if the municipalities needed aid, should find the ways and means themselves. I always took the position that if a province found that its business was in such shape that it could not meet its demands in relation to the needs of the municipalities, then the federal government would be ready to come to the assistance of that province, but without the province so stating in the first instance, we would expect the municipalities and the provinces to look after their own unemployed. What happened? In a very short time, instead of more and more money being paid out of the federal treasury on unemployment relief, payments ceased altogether, and during the ten years from the time that the Conservative administration started this system of paying out public money from the federal treasury to assist the provinces to help the municipalities, there was not a total of $2,000,000 spent. That was the position when the present administration took office. During the period we were in office the amount that was spent from the federal treasury was only a part of this; I am speaking from memory on that point, but I know that over the whole ten years the amount did not come to $2,000,000.
What took place at the time of the change of government? My right hon. friend in the campaign of 1930 stated in all parts of the country that the problem of unemployment

Relief Act, 1934

in Canada was such that it was no longer merely a municipal problem, no longer a provincial problem; he said it was a national problem, and that if he were returned to power he was going to deal with it as a national problem and was going to call a special session of parliament for that purpose. Parliament was summoned to meet in September, 1930, to deal with the problem of unemployment. My right hon. friend brought in his measure of unemployment relief. What did 'he ask this house to do? To give him $2,000,000? No. He asked the house to vote him $20,000,000 for the purpose of unemployment relief. But, he said, in connection with this unemployment relief we are not going to ask for any audit of the accounts; we are going to pay this money over to the provinces, and when we get the receipt of the province that is all we shall expect. That is what he said to the country; that is what people in all parts of the dominion understood-that the federal government would have fulfilled its obligation when it voted sums of money and turned them over to the provinces and obtained the certificate of the province indicating that the money had been received and properly dealt with. I said at the time to the Prime Minister that the problem was a totally different one from what it had been theretofore; that we were facing a very critical situation, a depression likely to laslt for several years, and that it was advisable that at the outset he adopt measures which *would ensure careful supervision and federal control over federal moneys. The Prime Minister says he asked the opposition to cooperate, and I then made the concrete suggestion that I have read to the committee to-night. The Prime Minister's reply was that to adopt such a course would be an insult. 3 said to the Prime Minister-I have not the words before me, but they will be found in the 1930 Hansard-that he would rue the day that he refused to provide for any kind of federal supervision over the expenditure of federal moneys. That day has now come. But it has not come to the extent that it is coming, with respect to this vast waste in the expenditure of public money.
Let me recall another instance to make clear what was said at the time. Knowing something about the Department of Labour and the extent to which it was equipped to carry on its own business without having additional obligations thrust upon it, I suggested to the Prime Minister that neither the Department of Labour nor any other department of government could begin to deal with the great national problem of unemployment

as part of its ordinary routine business. I pointed out that the Department of Labour was not equipped for it; that its business was to carry on the work of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act and of the Combines Investigation Act, to prepare for publication the Labour Gazette, and so on; that the time of every man of the staff and of the minister was already fully occupied, and that the situation was wholly analogous to what had arisen during the war when additional obligations were thrown on certain departments. I begged him to adopt the same policy with respect to unemployment relief as was adopted by the war administration with respect to the problems then arising, in setting up the food board, the imperial munitions board, the fuel board; and I suggested that in regard to unemployment relief we should have a national commission, just as in war time we had the national patriotic fund organization, broadly representative of the interests of capital and the interests of labour and organizations such as chambers of commerce and boards of trade, the Salvation Army, the National Council of Women, the Red Cross, and the like, that have to do with these great questions. I suggested that a representative body of that kind should be formed, given power under act of parliament, and made responsible to the government through the Minister of Labour for the way in which this relief should be carried out, coordinating the work of the, provinces and the municipalities. But that idea was scoffed at. I pointed out further that that was precisely what was done by the government of the day with respect to one relatively small matter that arose during the war, namely the disaster at Halifax, when an explosion took place which destroyed a considerable amount of property and human life. In dealing with that disaster the government of the day did not leave it to a department to administer the sums of relief money involved, they appointed a relief commission for the purpose. That outlay was properly audited; every dollar was traced; the commission did its work satisfactorily. I suggested that if that was advisable in regard to the relatively small expenditure there involved, surely when we were faced with a great national problem involving the whole of Canada, one which might continue for a series of years, something of the kind ought to have been done. What was the answer? The answer was:	The two things were not parallel; we were told a true parallel was to be found in what was done when Canada gave money to the Japanese at the time of the earthquake in that country. What we did

Relief Act, 1934
then, it was pointed out, was to send the money to Japan through the auditor general's department; the auditor general was to get a certificate from the Japanese government that the money had been spent for the purpose for which it was sent, and it was not our business to look further into the matter to see how Japan had spent the money. A certificate from the Japanese government was all that was necessary. The Prime Minister said: That is what we are going to do with regard to the provinces. We propose to give them this money, to get their receipt in due form that the money has gone for the purpose for which it was intended, and that is as far as we are going to look. The auditor general, like every one else, was doubtless led to believe that that was all that he was to look into, and that I imagine is why the auditor general has taken the stand he has taken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not what he said.

It was said on the floor of the house by the Prime Minister himself that what the government intended was to see that a certificate was given by the governments of the provinces that they had received the money from the auditor general's department, and that these moneys had been properly spent, and that the auditor's functions did not go beyond that. That is all on record; we do not have to go into any secret correspondence or interviews that none of us have heard of until to-night to discover what the policy of the government was. It was stated on the floor of the house, and in the words that I have given. It was stated again to-night by the Prime Minister himself when he said: We did not agree to deal with municipalities. Do you wonder, then, Mr. Chairman, that the auditor general, after the Prime Minister may have reversed in secret, as he says he did, the attitude that he took in public, and gave the auditor general certain instructions, that the auditor general might feel that he could not go beyond what the Prime Minister had stated to parliament itself was all he was expected to do? Parliament had voted these moneys as moneys to be paid simply to the provinces. It was not the fault of the auditor general that the money was to go only to the provinces and as stated by the Prime Minister not to be traced any further.
The position we on this side took was that with relation to the expenditure of public money the government should be responsible to the last cent, responsible no matter where these moneys went, or whether or not they were mixed up with the moneys of the prov-74726-125J
inces or the municipalities. The government cannot get away from that at the present time. That was the whole cause of the battle at the beginning and has been in every session since-the government seeking to relieve itself of responsibility by saying: We are dealing only with the provinces; we have nothing to do with the municipalities. If that is the ground they have taken from the outset, which they now take, they cannot blame the auditor general for not going further. They say: We have never dealt with municipalities; we are dealing only with provinces. No wonder the auditor general replies that he should not be interfering in municipal affairs. Nevertheless as a servant of parliament it is the duty of the auditor general to the extent that he may find it possible and deem it necessary, to see where federal moneys are going, and evidently he has done his duty by making a few tests of different municipalities, with results that to-day are only too well known in all parts of the country.
No; the mistake is this, and it is wholly the responsibility of the government, that the government itself, while it assumed office on the distinct understanding that it intended to make the problem of unemployment relief a national problem and to deal with it as such, the moment it came into office reversed that position and said: We will not regard this as a national problem; we propose to regard it as a matter for the provinces and the municipalities, and it is the business of the provinces not our business to look after how moneys may be spent by municipalities. The government washed its hands of the whole business and just issued the cheques. That is the situation; no exception can be taken to the aocurancy of what I have said. It is for that reason and that only that we have the shameful situation that is gradually coming to be known to the puiblic to-day. I say to the Minister of Labour I do not believe that in any of the agreements he has had with the provinces he has included the clause that the auditor general of Canada should have the right and that it would be his duty or that of his officers to follow the expenditure of moneys to the last payment, and that the receipts would be expected from recipients of public money indicating the fact that money had been duly received by them, and that the federal government was giving this money only on one condition, namely, that it was to go for the support of those who are out of employment, and for them only; that it was not to go for the purchase of supplies, or for the payment of expenses of administration or towards materials used by contractors, or to replace
Relief Act, 1934

federal or provincial outlays, but that it was to go simply for the relief of actual unemployment. I say that without that specific agreement with the provinces we could not expect anything else.
The Prime Minister has said to-night, "I believe the municipalities are honest; I believe the provinces are honest;" and so on. This afternoon the minister read us a statement about something which was supposed to be happening in British Columbia. He said, "Is this not the kind of thing common to both sides?" It was the very fact that everyone knew, human nature being what it is, that it was necessary to take the position which hon. members on this side took at the very outset with respect to the manner in which the expenditure of these public moneys was to be safeguarded. To tell the country that every dollar that the federal government was going to expend would be spent without any audit, so far as the federal treasury was concerned, was to invite all the kind of thing which is to be found in connection with officials who deal with public funds in a loose way. To hand over federal moneys raised by one body through taxation to be spent by other bodies having nothing to do with the raising of such moneys is fundamentally wrong in principle. That is another position which hon. members on this side asserted very strongly.
I should have concluded what I had begun to say a minute ago about the amount of money the government asked for at the first session. I have said that in the ten years preceding that session the total required towards the assistance of provinces and municipalities in connection with unemployment relief did not amount to $2,000,000. But the Prime Minister at the special session asked for $20,000,000 to extend over a period of only six months, namely, until the following March. I said to him at the time that he was asking for a sum of money far greater than he would require, and I believe he found difficulty in expending this large sum,-I know he did. But what did he do next session? He took another step which was inviting a still greater waste of public money. He took the step which the minister is now proposing to repeat and against which we protested on the occasion to which I am referring. On that occasion, he said. "We will not ask for any special amount, but will make our demands unlimited. In other words, we will ask for a blank cheque, and issue all the money we please." Knowing human nature I wonder if we could expect that the public money would be other than wasted when the government said, "Give us a blank cheque;

we will not be satisfied with any fixed amount; we want power to spend all that we please," and when in addition the Prime Minister announced there would be no audit by the auditor general, because such audit would be an insult to the provinces.
It would be ridiculous not to expect the very thing that has happened. At each session hon. members on this side have drawn attention to the vicious character of that type of legislation, namely, of voting sums of money without any control by parliament or by its servants over the expenditures of those moneys. We have now before us only the fringe of what may be expected if an investigation into these matters is gone into. I say that after the Prime Minister's statement to-night about the auditor general, he owes it to this parliament to have a public investigation into the whole question of the expenditure of relief moneys, so as to give the auditor general a chance to come before hon. members of this house and explain his position. In that way we may be able to find out from the provinces, the municipalities and others just how this money has been spent, and why it was spent in the manner I have described.
This matter cannot be covered up by the government simply saying we adopted a certificate used by a previous administration. I pointed out that in taking office in 1921 the Liberal administration merely completed part of the work which had been undertaken by a previous administration, a work of assisting provinces and municipalities to re-establish men from overseas in positions of civil life. But we never adopted any emergency legislation such as this, which has now run for four years. If to-day the Prime Minister holds up a certificate and states, "This is what we have done; this is the certificate." I say it is not sufficient and it is not what should have been done to protect the public treasury.
I believe what has been said to-night gives the opposition more justification than ever, when we reach the clause in the bill which asks again for a blank cheque, to ask that the clause be amended, to read, "such sums of money as may be appropriated by this parliament." Those sums should be appropriated by parliament in specific terms, and we should expect them to be audited by the auditor general. And, similarly, I believe we have reason to expect the administration to meet the requests which we have been making as strongly as we could make them, namely, that this power now being sought to give to the government the power to pass under the heading of peace, order and good government any

Relief Act, 1934
order in council it pleases, should be dropped from the bill. That is the section we are now discussing, and I hope the minister even yet will see his way clear to delete the section.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I wonder if the right hon. gentleman will explain why he dealt with old age pensions just on the basis he did. I have had more scandals brought to my attention in connection with old age pensions than I have had in connection with the whole of unemployment relief. And he fathered it. Why? Why did he hand over all these moneys to the provinces? Why? Why did he not ask that there should be an audit such as 'he now asks for in these matters, at a time when he dealt with old age pensions? What are the frauds? What are the frauds that people are making? What about a man standing in a bank in western Canada during the last twenty-four months and finding a person cashing an old age pension cheque with one hand and cutting off coupons with the other? Why can the right hon. gentleman not be consistent? Why have we not a little of that milk of human kindness of which you so often talk? I say to the right hon. gentleman: why did he and his ministers and his government put forward the old age pensions in the form in which they did? Remember this, that the reason given now by the right hon. gentleman and his supporters was a reason which I thought was a fairly good one, that every time there was fraud, half of it fell upon the province. Now it would be seventy-five per cent against the dominion and twenty-five per cent against the province.
I just say in answer to everything that has been said to-night with respect to the administration in these matters that the reason we did not deal with the municipalities is that they are the creatures of the legislatures, and the contact between the federal government and the provincial government or outside institutions is with the provincial government. And every dollar, as it is claimed, and has been said in this house, that has been taken from the federal taxpayer means that two dollars were taken from the provincial or municipal taxpayer. Is that not some safeguard? Should it not be some safeguard? In view of what the right hon. gentleman has said, I cannot set up a committee to-morrow morning with regard to this matter, for as I observed the auditor general has to appear before a committee in another place for the purpose of making his statement with respect to public expenditures. And until that is complied with, I think it is sufficient for the moment. I see that he is to be examined by
the Senate committee of which Senator Robinson is the head, touching public expenditures. It is all right, you see, when you start it, when it is on your initiative; but it is all wrong when we start it. We took steps that were never taken by our predecessors to safeguard the expenditures. But to say that there is a great scandal behind all this is a reflection on the honour and honesty of Canadians. It may well be that Canadians, as was said to-night, have been prosecuted for fraud in taking relief, but did hon. gentlemen observe that it was not fraud against the dominion, but fraud against the province or against the municipality? There is not a case in which there was any allegation of fraud against the dominion, because we did not deal with them individually. We dealt with the province, and if a province has defrauded us we will get the money back. To say that the Dominion government should follow down every individual payment by a province for relief directly or otherwise, I simply say I do not believe that would be the thought of any intelligent person engaged in any business. The local authorities, the municipalities first, and then the provinces, must deal with them.
I want to be perfectly frank and say that when the right hon. gentleman with his experience of nine years as Prime Minister made the statement that he did in. 1930, I merely made my observations as a business man that I believed that if we had the certificates of the auditors of the provinces that would be ample for me, and that we should not follow the money into the hands of the provinces because these were grants in aid; and the statute so says. The right hon. gentleman himself so stated long prior to 1930.
I put this single consideration before the committee: Making as we believed adequate provision for the safeguarding of the expenditures of these moneys in the hands of the provinces, with a form of certificate whi-rfi went at least three steps further than the former certificate to safeguard the federal' treasury, and with the approval of the auditor general, I must say that after reading of these prosecutions I .became very much concerned about the situation. The right hon. gentleman had had nine years of experience as Prime Minister, while I was speaking more from business experience; and when the house had risen, we had a gathering of the cabinet next morning-we were up all night-and I did request with all the earnestness I could that extraordinary care be taken to see that we would get the certificates so that we could feel safe with respect to the expenditures. The certi* ficate will appear in Hansard to-morrow and
Relief Act, 1934

will indicate I think that it is the safeguard that any ordinary business man would take with respect to matters of this kind.
I do still say to the members of this committee that no federal government can undertake to guarantee the honesty of every individual receiving relief. A case of fraud in obtaining a pension came up at Regina the other day. It was one of the earliest pensions, yet it was found that assistance had been given to a mother because of the loss of a child, and it turned out that she had some $12,000 although she had alleged that hers was a case of poverty. I saw it only in the newspapers, as I suppose other hon. gentlemen did. Steps were 'taken to have the money refunded to the crown. You have cases of that kind, and cases innumerable that I might mention in connection with old age pensions and other matters. But when we put into the hands of the provincial authority our proportion of the moneys under the agreement, and the provincial auditor certifies that the expenditures have been made and that the municipalities have complied with their obligations, then I do submit that if there has been fraud or irregularities we will get it out of the provinces; we will keep it out of any moneys that may be coming to them. There need be no question about that.
It is all right to say that the auditor general cannot speak for himself, but he seems to be able to write for himself, and after a few test audits, if under these circumstances he has made no answer to the request that was made by the Minister of Labour for the purpose of having the matter dealt with, what is the reason. Why did he make the observation he did about Port Alfred, that it might embarrass the municipality if he was asked to do it? I have a right to know; I do not know, and no one can get it from him.
When it is suggested that the auditor general took his cue from what might have been said in this parliament, the answer is that he was asked if a form of certificate prepared in exactly the opposite sense was satisfactory or not, and he replied, not indeed immediately but after taking solme time, that it was satisfactory. Let us be fair about this matter. Under these circumstances, if the responsibility rests anywhere, then if it is not where I have indicated I cannot understand what Vesponsibility means.
We have paid under the terms of agreements to the provinces, and not to municipalities, sums of money which were the subject matter of agreements, based upon payments being made for the same work in part by municipalities and in part by the provinces. In the city of Montreal case we have not yet

received the certificate; the minister and his accountants have been waiting for months for the certificate that will enable them to make payments, and when we receive the certificate over the signature of a provincial auditor and a minister of the province we shall make the payments. Is there any other way in which you could carry out the very principles which the right hon. gentleman supported so strongly in this house prior to the election of 1930, namely, that the constitutional obligation was one thing, the national character of the disaster was another, and the national character of the disaster involved the granting of assistance to the provinces? Those sums of money we have paid to the provinces when and as certificates in the form I have indicated were produced to enable payments to be made.
With respect to the question of a limitation being placed upon the expenditures to be made, we did one year place a limitation, and I am bound to say that it was not as satisfactory as when there was no limitation, because, just as soon as it was apparent that there was a certain sum of money available for the purpose, the provinces combined and said: That is exactly the sum we want. It was not a combination open and apparent, but they would-shall I say?-adjust their difficulties so that they synchronized, to use a well-known word, with the amount of money available. We desire to make the amount available as small as possible, and if it is thought that that proposal will better serve the purpose in mind and the purpose set out in the bill, we will consider what amount might be provided.
I shall not deal further with the other matters referred to by the right hon. gentleman under peace, order and good government except to say that he said that I had omitted to deal with the position in connection with the president of the United States. That is perfectly true. I did not think it required any discussion in this house. The real truth is that the only difference between the United States and Canada is that in Canada the executive is the governor in council. That means that a majority of council must agree to a certain line of action being taken. The executive in the United States is one man, and one only. He signs, and that is the end of it. The safeguards here are first of all the number of the advisers in council. Secondly, the powers that were conferred upon the president of the United States were in some cases for two years. Other powers that were conferred upon him were without any time limit. Some were for a shorter period than two

Relief Act, 1934
years. With respect to his power to make trade agreements the limit is three years. Other legislation is limited, some by a shorter term and some by a longer. But there is one clear distinction, the only one which need be considered in dealing with a matter of this kind, the executive of the United States is the president himself whereas the executive here is the governor in council. The governor in council means every member or the majority of the members of the council, the minority accepting the view of the majority in the action arrived at. That is the only difference, and the only matter which need be mentioned in reference to this question. That is so far as I can see it at the moment or so far as it affects the matter. The powers conferred upon the president are so far beyond the powers which it is suggested should be conferred on our executive that they are not in any sense in the same class.
I mention this because I said this afternoon that we regret that we cannot meet the views of the opposition and leave out the provision with respect to peace, order and good government. I should like to put this test, with which I think the right hon. gentleman will agree. Supposing in 1931, when we were asking for these powers, I had been asked a question similar to that asked this afternoon: "Why do we need it?" If I had said that I wanted it because I desired to restrict the export of gold and that England would go off the gold standard some time next September, hon. members would have laughed at me. I can give an illustration from my own experience. I happen to know that that summer a distinguished financier on this continent who was watching the trend of events cabled to a gentleman in London asking if in his opinion England would soon go off the gold standard. The gentleman in London cabled back that that was an absurd suggestion for him to make, and yet it happened in September. I use that merely by way of illustration.
There are other conditions which face the world at the moment and there is the talk which I deprecate greatly and which I fancy the right hon. gentleman deprecates more than I-the talk of war. I think no good puipose is served in the world at large by talking about war. I think it is a terrible thing and it should be terrible in the sense in which it is used. That- is only my personal view. I know there is a statute which can be brought into force by proclamation but I think on reconsideration the members of this committee, when left to their own devices, would conclude that it is desirable in the national interest that the executive, which is the governor in council, should have the power to
pass such orders in council as may be necessary for the .peace, order and good government of the country. I shall not enlarge upon what I said this afternoon except to say that the seeking of this power obviously serves no personal interest. It cannot add to one's happiness but it makes one feel a little more certain that in the event of a crisis he has the machinery with which to protect the national life of the country.

I should like to follow the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in the reverse order to that in which he spoke, taking up the last point first. He has just asked what he possibly could have done with regard to the export of gold if that question had been asked two years ago and where without disclosing his hand he could have obtained the legislation necessary to help to meet a situation of that kind. I would reply by saying that he did not need anything more than will be left in this bill if he agrees to strike out the very clause which he says it is necessary for him to retain, namely, the one giving the power, notwithstanding any statute or existing law, to pass orders in council under the heading of peace, order and good government. There would still remain this clause:
-take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect and maintain, the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof.
I ask the right hon. gentleman: Could anything be needed beyond that? If that is the purpose of the clause, what more could he needed? The section would still read:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council may take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect and maintain the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof.
We are perfectly agreeable to having that provision in the section remain, and I submit that that is all the right hon. gentleman *needs to have in order to deal with any financial situation or any situation affecting the credit of this country. In view of what the Prime Minister has just said, I submit that the other clause should not be permitted to remain.
The Prime Minister deprecates the mention of the word "war." I agree with him and I hope the time will never come when this parliament will have again to discuss war. But if it ever has to discuss war, I submit that is the time above all others when parliament should be called together and the decision as to the action to be taken not left to the governor in council. If the Prime Min-
Relief Act, 1934

ister is retaining this clause which deals with peace, order and good government in order that he may have the power, notwithstanding any statute or law, to have this country participate in a war, there is a stronger reason than ever why the clause should be stricken out. I do not know that that is what is in his mind, but he has raised the question himself. I have no wish to discuss the question of war in this connection, but it has been discussed in this parliament at different times. My recollection is that a resolution was passed some sessions ago to the effect that in the event of the possibility of war parliament should be summoned before any forces of Canada were placed at the disposition of His Majesty to serve at any point outside of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is in a statute.

The Prime Minister reminds me that that is in a statute, and that statute should be observed. But this clause states that notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law which includes the very statute just referred to, the governor in council may take whatever steps he deems necessary to deal with peace, order and good government. I submit that the Prime Minister has just given two additional reasons this evening why that power should not be left in the hands of the governor in council.
Let me come to another matter referred to by the Prime Minister. He said that the only difference between the executive of the United States and the executive of Canada was that the executive of the United States was one man while the executive of Canada was the majority of the ministers in council. If I wanted to refine the point I could remind the Prime Minister that under the British constitution the executive is one man. The sovereign is the executive, but in Canada as elsewhere in British countries, the king is advised by his ministers, of whom the Prime Minister is chief. The president of the United States is one man, but he also is surrounded by members of a cabinet and undoubtedly any major action he takes is in accordance with the views of the majority of his cabinet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

Not necessarily, possibly, but I submit he would be very foolish if he did not act in accordance with the views of the majority of his cabinet, and I think he does on most occasions. However, the fundamental difference is not what the Prime Minister has said it is, the difference between one man and half a dozen. So far

as the United States is concerned, the executive has no place in congress and cannot make his views known by discussion and argument, whereas under the British system the executive as represented by the ministry not only has its place in parliament, but is responsible to parliament for every act and must get its majority from parliament itself. The president of the United States may choose whom he wishes as his cabinet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He 'has to get a majority in congress.

He has not to find seats for his ministers and is not responsible to his congress in the way in which a prime minister is here. If he wants to deal with any question he has to get the authority needed for the purpose from congress somehow, but he gets that without his having to discuss the why and wherefore of his policy on the floor of parliament as the Prime Minister must and is able to do. The situation is entirely different.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He reads a message, that is all.

Yes, but my
right hon. friend can come here and with his powers of debate and eloquence he can persuade his following to give him anything he wants. He can give his followers the reasons why he should get these particular powers- no one knows it better than he-and they will give him anything he wants. The president of the United States has not that power; he has to rely upon what congress will give him when it is in session. There is a complete difference between the two, so that if anything in the form of action required to meet an emergency is required, the president of necessity has to have when congress is not in session certain powers which the Prime Minister does not begin to need to have, for the simple reason that he can get whatever powers he likes, in advance of the prorogation of parliament, or if he wishes to bring parliament together at any moment he can do so immediately in order to get these powers.
Now to return to the other matter we were discussing, the question of relief, the Prime Minister again seeks to draw a herring across the trail. He asks, "With regard to old age pensions, why did you not make a different provision from the one you did? We were simply doing the same kind of thing in regard to unemployment relief as you did in regard to old age pensions." Well, I would say that if we made a mistake in regard to old age pensions that is no reason why he should make the same mistake.

Relief Act, 1934

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But you did not say it was a mistake.

I did not say that. I will answer my right hon. friend this way. The reason we dealt with old age pensions in the way we did was that the requirements of the British North America Act left the matter of old age pensions exclusively in the hands of the provinces under the head of property and civil rights.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And relief in the same way.

No, that is where I do not agree with my right hon. friend; I say that it is not the same. There is nothing to support his statement. The right hon. gentleman said himself, during the campaign, that relief was a national problem; it was no longer provincial or municipal but was national. It was therefore for him to make it national, to be dealt with in that way, in view of the policy he declared. Moreover, when he spent money for purposes of relief he could attach to that expenditure any conditions he pleased. To show how far short of attaching such conditions-
Was not that true of old age pensions?
No, it was not true of old age pensions.
Was it not true that the government could attach any conditions they wished in reference to that matter?
No, there were restrictions because the question of old age pensions involved certain considerations respecting property and civil rights.
So does this.

No, this does
not, and that is the difference. This is a sum of money which the government is spending for a specific purpose which it names.
And it involves civil rights.

Just as the
Prime Minister himself said, we could give money to Japan, and if we could give money to Japan we could give money to the governments of the provinces of Canada.
Old age pensions involved civil rights.

If my hon.
friend wants to make a speech he will have time to do so.
We don't want the committee misled.

It will never be misled by anything my hon. friend says.
I should like if I might to continue without interruptions.
I wish to remind the Prime Minister of what was said in this very connection with respect to these grants in aid-and here may I say that the Prime Minister has been kind enough to observe that having occupied for a number of years the position which he now fills one gains a certain amount of experience, and I trust that this experience, by whomsoever it is obtained, will be of value in public life at all times. And out of that experience, when this country was faced with the problem of unemployment on a vast scale and the possibility of depression running over a period of years, with the likelihood of the provinces being unable to meet their various obligations, I urged at the very first session that these grants in aid to the provinces should be stopped pending the calling of a conference between the dominion and provincial governments to see whether it was not possible to have some arrangement made whereby the dominion could assume a large number of obligations for relief in its different forms-social insurance in its various aspects -taking them over as a national obligation and in return obtaining agreements from the provinces to amend their powers of taxation in some directions, or making concessions with respect to future subsidies. My hon. friends opposite will remember that I spoke over and over again about the inevitable consequences of continuing grants in aid at a time like this, pointing out that they meant that sooner ot later the public treasury would be depleted beyond all expectation. I was hooted at by hon. gentlemen opposite for repeating this observation so often, but the force of it is coming home to them now when it is too late. I suggested then that we should seek an amendment to the British North America Act inasmuch as this question was likely to present itself with increasing urgency with time. I urged that we should at once take steps, in conference with the provinces, and by whatever course might be deemed necessary, to see whether the British North America Act could not be so amended as to give the federal government larger powers with respect to social and industrial legislation in order that we might have uniformity of laws throughout the dominion, the provinces being relieved of some obligations, having them made federal charges, and the provinces on their part foregoing, if that was
Reliej Act, 1934

equitable, their subsidies either in whole or in part. I made this suggestion with a view to bringing matters to such a point as to insure that the power raising taxation would be charged with the responsibility of its control and expenditure, instead of following the false principle of placing upon one government the obligation of raising taxes and allowing another government or series of governments and municipalities as well to spend the money, for the raising of which they had had no responsibility whatever.
On all these counts therefore it seems to me that the need is becoming stronger and stronger for compliance with the request made from this side of the house, even now at the eleventh hour, rather than that the present situation should continue, albeit for but a few months or a year, or whatever the period may be.
With reference to the auditor general's position, the Prime Minister says that he will consider the matter. I think we had better have the public accounts committee called together and have some of these matters gone into very fully there, so that we may find out how public moneys have 'been spent. It is high time the committee was called together. We might have the auditor general and others before the committee. I trust the Prime Minister will see that this is granted.
These I think were the main points referred to by my right hon. friend. I would add this, with respect to old age pensions, that the Liberal administration-and I presume the present administration is following the same course-did audit the accounts with respect to old age pensions so far as the provinces were concerned; they did have their own auditors and have always had supervision over the provincial governments' expenditures, and I believe that the auditor general has been free from time to time to make, and has actually made, test audits in regard thereto.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
What the
Prime Minister has just said about there being other public expenditures that are not being properly audited is, I think, only a further reason that now that the whole matter has come up for consideration and discussion in the way it has, we should seek to take immediately the steps that will prevent anything of this kind happening in the future. That is Why we are stressing the matter as strongly as we are in regard to this particular measure. My right hon. friend will do me the justice, I believe, to say that at no time have I advocated any concealment of inquiries into public matters of any kind, but that I have stressed as strenuously as I could full supervision and control by the House of Commons and by its servant over all public expenditures. If there has been one thing above another that I have been emphasizing each year, it has been the necessity of that complete control on the part of the House of Commons and the auditor general over all expenditures of public money, especially in dealing with the relief situation which is an abnormal one. In handling matters in times of emergency there is greater need than at any other time that those safeguards should be exercised with the greatest possible care. For that reason I hope when the minister under the present legislation is making his agreements with the

provinces, he will see to it that clauses are inserted which will ensure a more adequate following down the line of those public expenditures than has been the case heretofore and that eveiy dollar of federal money goes, not to administration or to contractors or to pay for supplies, or to relieve provinces and municipalities of their own obligations, but to labour itself, a satisfactory certificate of payment being obtained in receipt thereof.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The certificate may be
as incorrect as it is now alleged ours are.

That can be
followed up by federal officers. I should like to point this out to the Prime Minister: we are in the extraordinary situation that we have voted sums of money running to over $110,000,000 for expenditure on relief alone, and yet the house has no information as to the numbers of the unemployed. The Department of Labour has not this information. It has made all kinds of excuses and apologies for not having it. All it needed to have done was to require any province giving federal money to a municipality to obtain from that municipality a statement of the numbers of its unemployed. Those statements should be returnable periodically to the government and after being tabulated Should be brought to the attention of this house. We have had from Premier Pattullo a statement that the number of unemployed in British Columbia to-day is 100,000. British Columbia has a population about one-nineteenth of the rest of Canada, so it would look as though, if that were the average for all the provinces according to population, the total number of unemployed would be about 1,500,000. I think, however, British Columbia relatively has a larger number of unemployed than the other provinces; but if figures are available, we ought to know.
On what date was that?

In the press
of Saturday night there was a statement to the effect that there was something like
100.000	unemployed in British Columbia. If that province has been able to get those figures in so short a time, some of the other provinces ought to be able to get similar information. One* very simple way to get the figures is to insert such a provision in the agreements entered into by the minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid the statement in regard to the 100,000 unemployed is a guess. It may, however, have some reference to a matter to which I am going to direct the attention of the right hon. gentleman to indicate how difficult it is to deal with the situation in the way he suggests. Shortly after the change of government in British Columbia my attention was directed to a press clipping in which a notice was given that certain works w'ould go forward at a particular point. I will show it to the right hon. gentleman to-morrow. Membership in the Liberal association was a sine qua non.

That was
brought u,p this afternoon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I was not in then. That
indicates one of the difficulties experienced in matters of this kind. I would like to show the right hon. gentleman some of the efforts that have been made in the imposition of conditions on the provinces and the difficulty that has been experienced in connection with those payments which have not to do with labour but have to do with matters connected with the credit and interest obligations of the provinces. The prospect seems much easier viewed from the outside than it is from within.

Let us consider Newfoundland. I have only one thing to place before the committee to-night, and it is this: Last year I asked the Minister of Finance about the grants to Newfoundland. He told me that the Dominion government had guaranteed to certain banks the interest payment amounting to several hundred thousand dollars. On that occasion the opposition blamed the government for guaranteeing Newfoundland loans. The Minister of Finance was at that time very eloquent, and finally during the world conference when this dominion was asked to renew the guarantee or to give an additional one to Newfoundland, it refused to do so, and quite rightly. Therefore, as was pointed out during the debate on the address, it was not the members of the opposition who were wasting the time of the house in that matter, but the Minister of Finance himself.
The other day my right hon. leader spoke about those guarantees and the Minister of Finance pointed out that no money was loaned to Newfoundland; that it was only a guarantee that was given by this government. Therefore I would like to know from them whether the guarantee which was given to Newfoundland last year amounts to very much. To what banks was that guarantee given, and is it still in existence? Has the government been released from all its obligations towards the creditors of Newfoundland? May I point out at the same time that at page 9 of Hansard of this year it will be seen that I asked the government for the production of the Amulree report on New-

foundland and that the Prime Minister said that in that report there was nothing of interest to Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no.

For the information of the right hon. gentleman I will read what he said as reported at page 9 of Hansard:
Right Hon. R. B. Bennett (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, it was not proposed to table it. The report was not in any sense connected with the operations of this government. The government of Canada was asked to name a commissioner to sit with commissioners from Great Britain and Newfoundland. With that in mind Mr. Magrath was selected.
My idea in asking that was to know what had been found by those three gentlemen about Canada's obligation to the creditors of Newfoundland, and that was the only idea I had in view when I put the question. Therefore I will ask the government kindly to answer the questions that I have put and whether this is not the time to table that report which is just as interesting as that of Mr. Sutherland on the tobacco business.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The obligation of the dominion is represented by guarantees given to the chartered banks to the extent of
S625,000.	A half year's interest was being paid, and the British authorities said that they would guarantee or pay to the extent of one-half if we would the other. As the default of Newfoundland would have seriously affected our own securities, being trustee securities, we did so. The present position, since the commission has taken over, I am not in a position to state without verifying the facts. But that is the figure, $625,000.

I thank the right hon. gentleman for the information he has just given. If he had agreed to the tabling of the Amulree report it would not have been necessary for me to ask him any questions to-night. Therefore I ask if he will kindly reconsider what he said at the begininng of the session, and let the members of the house see that report, part of which has been published by the financial papers. It is a report which is of interest to all of us.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think copies of the report are in the library. I could not lay it on the table, because it is not a report that originated from any action taken by this house or this parliament. We have, I think, two or three copies, perhaps half a dozen; but surely there is a copy in the library. If there is not I will see that one of those we have is put there.
I thank the right hon. gentleman.
May I ask the Prime Minister if the guarantee or arrangement made for the building of Canada's legation at Toyko was made under the relief act, or in what way it was done?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My memory is, no. The order in council was passed finally when I was not in the country. I promised the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) that the papers would be brought down, and I thought it had been done already.

I made a motion for
them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The fact is that the minister to Japan himself advanced the money for the construction of the building, and is to be repaid as appropriations can be made for that purpose from time to time. In the meantime the interest on the money is not as much as would have been paid for rent. A high minded public service was rendered by the minister under an arrangement which merely contemplates his being repaid the money expended for construction in the manner I have indicated.
Do I understand that the financial transaction has been carried out by the Canadian minister himself, or was a guarantee given .to him in respect of those expenditures?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is covered by an agreement.
How was the loan arranged?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not know that that was disclosed. He is a man of means; I am not sure even that he borrowed the money. He put up his own money; that is the short way to put.

I would like to say a word before eleven o'clock. I hope the suggestion of the leader of the opposition that this matter be referred to the public accounts committee will be given effect to forthwith. This is a more serious matter than ordinary complaints made against a cabinet minister who is here to defend himself. The auditor general is an officer of this house, responsible only to us, and something very close to a charge of incompetence has been made against him, somewhat comparable to such a charge against the Speaker or the clerk of the house. I am wholly unwilling that the information I seek should be obtained in another house. We do

Canadian Legation in Japan
not know what scope that investigation is going to take, nor can we be there to direct it along the lines of the charges made here. As regards the necessity of a thorough investigation, we must recall that the test made has been quite superficial; it was very slight, touching only the high spots here and there. For instance, in British Columbia I understand it consisted of a comparatively slight investigation of accounts for the year 1933. If the auditor had gone back to 1931 things might have been revealed that would make your hair stand on end. It will be remembered that in 1932 the relief situation there came into the hands of the Fordham commission, under which a very genuine attempt was made by the province and the dominion to run things on right lines, But if the examination had gone back to 1931 we have only to recall the charges made by the dominion government's man, McGeough, which have never been proved untrue, to realize the scope of the graft that I firmly believe would be revealed.
The Prime Minister dealt more than once with the idea that our safeguard was that if there was any graft, for every dollar of which the dominion was robbed there would be two dollars against the province and the municipality. But that is not so, because the province looked after the cities; in fact I think the cities for the most part ran their relief honestly and fairly. The province saw that the cities did not rob them. But who was to see that the province did not rob us? It is said that there was a provincial auditor, a very reliable man, but his duty was to see that the cities did not rob the province; he had no obligation to see that the province did not rob the dominion-I use the coarse word. I gave an illustration of how it could be done without any misconduct on the part of the city. Excessive charges were made for hire of government trucks and machinery, and expenditures of a capital nature were charged which should not have been shared by the dominion. Those are things in connection with which the province was not robbed, the city did not rob anyone, but we were robbed, inasmuch as we were asked to pay a share of accounts which, to put it plainly, were padded. For instance, gasoline was charged with the six or eight cents provincial tax added to the price, and we were asked to pay our share of that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Was that wholly wrong?
I do not think the dominion should pay a provincial tax on gas.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is a question that was argued at great length. If anyone else had used it they would have had that revenue.

Then I shall not use that as an illustration, but I shall use that of supervising employees being put in, and excessive charges made for trucks and machinery. I think it would be in the interests of the government and of this house if this thing were thoroughly investigated before the public accounts committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have made some inquiry since I spoke. The difficulty of getting the public accounts committee together is that most of the members, I think twenty in all, are serving on the banking and commerce committee. The difficulty of getting a quorum, I am informed by the chief whip, has been very great. It is almost impossible, because of the interest taken in the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee. But I shall see what can be done.
Progress reported.
